work.heading: Four systems, four leaks that stopped.

cases.title: Debt collection over WhatsApp, for a multinational agro company
cases.body: Agents used to query invoices and send payment barcodes by hand, one customer at a time. Every minute a customer waited, they were more likely to abandon the process and buy from a competitor instead. I built a WhatsApp agent that authenticates the customer, pulls the invoice in real time, and sends the barcode with no person involved at any step. Built on AWS, with Lambda and DynamoDB doing the heavy lifting and Python underneath.

cases.title: A sales agent for Brazil's largest car dealership group
cases.body: Leads from the website for BYD and Toyota models were cooling off in the gap between form submission and a callback. Across dozens of locations, sales couldn't close that gap fast enough. The agent I built picks up the lead the moment the form is submitted, moves the conversation to WhatsApp, answers product questions, and books the dealership visit. It runs on Azure, with Databricks handling the data layer. I can't stand behind a clean conversion number here, since the client had no attribution instrumentation in place before this project, but the response-time change itself is real and measured.

plain.headline: Hours to seconds
plain.sub: lead response time, across multiple brands and locations

cases.title: A CRM-to-warehouse pipeline for Gal Capital
cases.body: The sales team ran entirely on Bitrix24, but nobody could see the funnel by team, by broker, or by deal, so leadership was making commission and staffing decisions blind. I built a pipeline from Bitrix24 into BigQuery, feeding two dashboards: one operational, for day-to-day management, and one executive, for the leadership view. Built on GCP, using Cloud Functions, PubSub, and Cloud Scheduler.

plain.headline: Two dashboards
plain.sub: team, broker, and deal-level visibility built from zero

cases.title: A support chatbot for Hotmart
cases.body: The support menu had no real model for what a bot should own versus hand off to a human, so requests just accumulated. I scoped it down deliberately: four features, three languages, chosen by what the data said actually mattered, not by what was easiest to build.

pattern.heading: None of the five roles above said "engineer." Here's why that's the wrong read.
paragraphs: Analyst. NLP specialist. PM for Chatbots. Senior PM for Data Ingestion. Founder. What the timeline above doesn't spell out is that the same person wrote the automation that recovered R$1.9M, the NLP tooling at Take Blip, and the production code behind a system moving R$4M a day, under titles that never said so. I see a problem, talk to whoever is stuck doing it by hand, map the rules underneath it, and build the thing that makes it disappear. That's been true since the first job, not since the one with "founder" in the title.

That's the actual edge: I can scope a product, define the KPIs, manage a team of developers, and write the implementation myself when that's faster. There's no handoff between the business problem and the technical solution. I am the handoff.
